title: A Strongly Subcubic Combinatorial Algorithm for Triangle Detection with Applications

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction (BMM paragraph) vs. Definitions and notations section
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states, right after discussing Bansal–Williams and Chan's combinatorial BMM algorithms: 'Here the Õ notation hides poly(loglog n) factors.' Later, in the Definitions and notations section, the paper explicitly redefines the notation: 'The Õ notation hides poly(log) factors, whereas the Ô notation hides poly(loglog) factors.' These two statements directly contradict each other — Õ cannot simultaneously hide poly(log n) factors (as stated in Definitions) and poly(loglog n) factors (as stated earlier for Bansal-Williams/Chan). This is an internal inconsistency in notation that a careful reviewer would require to be resolved (likely the earlier instance should have used Ô, not Õ).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section on Boolean product witness matrices (discussion following Theorem 3)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states: 'An elegant randomized algorithm due to Seidel [33]... computes a matrix of witnesses in time O(n^ω log n); if ω = 2, the runtime becomes O(n^2 log^2 n).' Substituting ω = 2 directly into O(n^ω log n) yields O(n^2 log n), not O(n^2 log^2 n). The stated runtime after substitution introduces an extra, unexplained factor of log n that is mathematically inconsistent with the formula given immediately before it.

predicted_errors.error_location: k-Clique section, paragraph beginning 'Obtaining faster than trivial combinatorial algorithms...'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'A slightly faster combinatorial algorithm was just announced in [3]' for k-clique immediately before claiming that the paper's own algorithm (O(n^{7k/9})) is 'providing the first solution to the above open problem' (obtaining more than polylogarithmic combinatorial speedups for k-clique). If reference [3] already announced a combinatorial algorithm beating the O(n^k/log^k n) bound (even 'slightly'), the claim of being the 'first' solution is logically in tension with the cited prior work, unless [3]'s improvement is only polylogarithmic (which is not clarified in the text), making the novelty claim potentially overstated or at least ambiguously justified.

The paper asserts without rigorous support that 'these results represent the greatest advance in triangle detection in over 45 years and the greatest advance in Boolean matrix multiplication in over 50 years.' This is a strong, subjective superlative claim presented as an established fact, not substantiated by any formal comparative metric in the paper beyond the authors' own assessment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Applications section, discussion of Chan [15] segment-intersection triangle detection
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text defines 'T_3(m) denotes the time complexity of finding a triangle in a graph with m edges' but then uses the notation 'Õ(T_3(n))' with argument n instead of m, creating a mismatch between the defined function's parameter (m, edges) and its actual invocation (n), without clarifying what n represents in that context (number of segments vs. edges of the auxiliary intersection graph).
